lessons.title: el teatro — a place for looking, and the word theory came from it
lessons.gloss: theatre — Greek theatron, a place for viewing, from theaomai "to behold"; the same root sits inside the English word theory

segments.text: You can already name el cine. Say it, then say the building people went to for two thousand years before there was any such thing.
el cine — the other place you go to watch something, and the one whose name is barely a century old.
stress-penultimate — te-A-tro, stress on the second of three. see reference.
r-tap — the r is one flick of the tongue, not a growl.
el teatro — "the theatre." Latin theatrum, from Greek théatron, "a place for viewing," built on theáomai, "to behold."
The Greeks named the building after what the audience does, not after what happens on the stage. A theatre is a looking-place.
Now the payoff. That same theá- gives Greek theōría — "a viewing, a contemplation" — which arrives in English as theory:
theatre, amphitheatre — the looking-place.
theory, theoretical — what you see when you look hard at something.
A theory and a theatre are the same idea twice: someone standing back and watching. Spanish keeps both, teatro and teoría, and they have never stopped being cousins.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: two names, two ages

segments.text: Set the two buildings beside each other:

utterances: place: el teatro. named after: what the audience does — viewing. age of the word: ancient Greek.
place: el cine. named after: what the machine does — writing movement. age of the word: about 1900.

segments.text: Both are masculine and both take el. One is among the oldest words in this book and one is among the newest, and you learned them a chapter apart.

segments.text: What did the Greeks name the theatre after — the stage, or the audience? (The audience: théatron is a place for viewing.) What everyday English word for an explanation shares that root? (Theory.)

lessons.title: la exposición — a putting-out
lessons.gloss: exhibition — Latin ex- "out" plus ponere "to place", a putting-out; the same ponere is inside compose, deposit and position

segments.text: You have el museo. A museum holds its collection all year. Say the word for the thing a museum puts on for three months and then takes down.
el museo — the building. This lesson is the event inside it.
accent-acute — the accent is on the last syllable: ex-po-si-CIÓN. see reference.
ci-th-s — the c before i is the soft one.
la exposición — "the exhibition." Latin expositio: ex- ("out") plus ponere ("to place"). An exhibition is literally a putting-out.
ponere is one of the most productive verbs Latin ever handed on. Once you see it, it is everywhere:
expose, exposition — placed out.
compose — placed together. deposit — placed down.
position, postpone, component, opponent.
Spanish has the verb itself, poner, "to put" — so exposición is transparent to a Spanish speaker in a way that exhibition is not to an English one.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the ending that tells you the gender

segments.text: Nouns ending in -ción are feminine, without exception worth worrying about.
la exposición, la habitación, la nación. The ending comes from Latin -tio, which was feminine, and Spanish kept the gender along with the sound.
That makes -ción one of the few endings you can trust on sight — most noun gender has to be learned with the word, and this one does not.

lessons.title: el circo — the ring, and the two c's in one word
lessons.gloss: circus — Latin circus "ring", from Greek kirkos; the ring is the oldest part of the idea and the only part still round

segments.text: Circo has two c's and they are not the same sound. Before reading on, say the word and listen to which one is soft.
ci-th-s — the first c, before i, is soft. see reference.
c-hard — the second c, before o, is hard, as in cat.
stress-penultimate — CIR-co.
One word, one letter, two jobs. The vowel that follows decides, every time.
el circo — "the circus." Latin circus, "a ring," borrowed from Greek kírkos. The Romans' Circus Maximus was a ring you raced around; the tent came much later and kept the shape and the name.
The family is large and all of it is round:
circle, circuit, circular, circumference.
circa — "around" a date.
Spanish cerca ("near") and cercar ("to surround") come from the same ring.
So a circus is not named for clowns or animals. It is named for the shape of the floor.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the rule you can see inside one word

segments.text: Most words make you check the letter against the vowel that follows it. Circo does the checking for you, because it contains both cases:

utterances: letter: cir-. followed by: i. sound: soft.
letter: -co. followed by: o. sound: hard.

segments.text: Keep this word as your reference. Whenever you are unsure how a c should sound, say circo and listen to which half matches.

segments.text: Which c in circo is soft and why? (The first — it is followed by i.) What does the Latin circus mean, and which English words keep it? (A ring: circle, circuit, circa.)

lessons.title: cinco lugares — five places, sorted by what their names describe
lessons.gloss: five places to go — the two you had and the three now beside them, sorted by what each name describes

segments.text: Name the five places you can now go to. Say them out loud before reading the list.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: what each name is actually about

segments.text: Every one of these buildings is named after something different, and once you sort them that way they stop being a list to memorise:

utterances: place: el teatro. named after: the audience. the thing itself: a looking-place.
place: el cine. named after: the machine. the thing itself: a movement-writer.
place: el museo. named after: the Muses. the thing itself: a seat of the arts.
place: la exposición. named after: the act. the thing itself: a putting-out.
place: el circo. named after: the floor. the thing itself: a ring.

segments.text: Two are named for people (the audience, the Muses), one for a machine, one for an action, and one for a shape. Not one of them is named for the art that happens inside it.

lessons.title: ¿Vamos al teatro o al circo? — the five places in a real question
lessons.gloss: putting the five places to work in a question, where al and a la do the choosing

segments.text: A place you can name is not yet a place you can propose. Ask a friend whether they want to go to the theatre or the circus, out loud, before reading on.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: al and a la, doing the gender work for you

segments.text: Proposing an outing needs a ("to") in front of the place, and the article comes along:
¿Vamos al teatro? — masculine, so a + el squeezes into al. ¿Vamos a la exposición? — feminine, so the two words stay apart.
Four of your five places take al. Only la exposición takes a la, and you can predict which without remembering, because -ción told you the gender when you met the word.
Every word here is one you have met:
—¿Vamos al cine? —No. Vamos al teatro. —¿Y el sábado? —El sábado, a la exposición del museo. Y el domingo, al circo. —¿Y después del circo? —Después, a bailar.
Four places, one short exchange, and the only thing you had to decide each time was al or a la.
The last line is the exception that proves it. Bailar is a verb, not a place, so it takes plain a and no article at all — the same reason me gusta bailar needed none.
